Renewals and Expansion

The Commercial SystemPart 24

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 12 October 2026 · 9-minute read · Revenue

Renewals and expansion are how a firm grows revenue from customers it already has. For most mid-size B2B firms the existing base is barely growing on its own: a KeyBanc and Sapphire Ventures survey of more than 100 private SaaS companies put median net revenue retention at about 101% and gross retention at about 90%. The firms that do better treat renewal as a process with a calendar, not a contract date. They decide each renewal months ahead, choose the expansion motion that fits the account's signals and record the reason for every renewal decision, so the next cohort can be predicted rather than hoped for.

New logos get the attention. Existing customers get the revenue. For a firm selling recurring services or software, the renewal date is the point at which most of next year's revenue is already decided, and expansion is the cheapest growth it can buy. Yet in many mid-size firms renewal is handled by whoever owns the contract, 30 days before it expires, and expansion happens when a customer asks.

The explainers on net revenue retention and customer health scoring cover the metrics. This piece covers the operating practice: the calendar, the choice of expansion motion and the record that connects them.

Most bases barely grow on their own

The benchmarks are sobering. The KeyBanc Capital Markets and Sapphire Ventures survey of private SaaS companies, published in October 2024 and covering more than 100 firms with a median annual recurring revenue of about $26m, reported median net revenue retention of about 101% and gross retention of about 90%. In plain terms, the typical firm lost about a tenth of its starting revenue each year to churn and downgrades, and won back only slightly more through expansion.

SaaS Capital's 2025 benchmarks for private B2B companies found that the median net retention for firms with annual contract values of $25,000 to $50,000 was 102%, with a top quartile of 111% and a bottom quartile of 97%. Firms with net retention of at least 110% grew faster than the 24% median growth rate in its sample; those below 100% grew more slowly. Growth Unhinged's 2025 benchmark of more than 800 mostly US software firms found that companies combining high net retention with low customer acquisition payback averaged 71% growth, against 10% for those with the opposite profile.

The case for retention goes beyond software. Frederick Reichheld's work at Bain, set in financial services, argued that a 5% increase in customer retention could produce more than a 25% increase in profit, because long-standing customers cost less to serve, buy more over time and refer others. The figure is old and sector-specific, but the mechanism applies to most recurring B2B relationships.

Why renewals are lost late

Most renewals are not lost in the renewal conversation. They are lost months earlier, and the firm finds out at the end.

Size is a poor guide to who will grow. Gartner's 2021 survey of 69 chief sales officers found that 58% of B2B sales organisations missed quota on key accounts, and that customers elevated to key-account status mainly because of large spend were 51% less likely to increase that spend over time. Key-account managers reporting high cross-functional collaboration saw about three times the spend from their key customers. The accounts that grow are the ones the whole firm works with, not simply the largest.

Experience is a reason to leave. McKinsey's 2024 research on B2B buyers found that more than half said they were likely to switch suppliers if they did not have a smooth experience across channels. Among those likely to switch, 54% cited poor digital experiences and 51% cited not being connected to the right person for help. Both show up in support tickets and account conversations long before the renewal date.

Regulation is also shortening the notice a supplier gets. The EU Data Act's switching rules for data processing services, which include SaaS, IaaS and PaaS, have applied since 12 September 2025. According to Cooley's summary, customers can switch with a maximum notice period of two months, porting must normally be completed within 30 days, and switching and data egress charges must be removed from 12 January 2027. Providers outside the EU are covered if they serve EU customers. For a supplier with EU customers, a long notice clause is no longer a dependable early warning.

Run renewals on a calendar

The fix is to make renewal a process that starts well before the contract date, with fixed checkpoints and an owner at each.

Days before renewalStepOwnerOutput
180Account review: usage, outcomes against the original case, health score, open issuesAccount ownerA renewal risk rating and a draft expansion hypothesis
120Value review with the customer: what was achieved, what is nextAccount owner with delivery leadAgreed outcomes for the next term, named sponsor confirmed
90Renewal decision recorded internally: renew as is, renew with change, expand or prepare for lossRevenue leaderA decision record with reason and expected outcome
60Commercial proposal sent, including any price change and expansion optionAccount owner and deal deskA proposal that follows the firm's proposal standard
30Signature, or escalation if not on trackAccount owner, executive sponsor if neededSigned renewal or an escalation decision
AfterOutcome written back, including reasons for churn or downgradeRevenue operationsUpdated record and health score inputs

The 90-day decision is the step most firms lack. It forces the firm to state what it expects to happen and why, which is the only way to know later whether its view of the account was right. Contracts with shorter notice periods, including those now covered by the Data Act, simply move the calendar earlier.

The value review at 120 days matters because renewals are decided on outcomes, not activity. The customer should be able to say what the last term achieved in their terms. If the account owner cannot, the renewal is at risk regardless of the health score.

A renewal is decided long before the contract date. The firm just finds out on the contract date.

Choose the expansion motion by signal

Expansion is not one motion. Each form needs a different signal and carries a different risk, and choosing the wrong one can put the renewal itself at risk.

Expansion motionSignal that it fitsMain riskWho leads
Price increase at renewalOutcomes delivered and documented; price below current listTriggers a competitive reviewAccount owner with finance
More seats, usage or volumeUsage near the contracted limit; new teams asking for accessLow engagement among existing usersAccount owner
Cross-sell of another service or productA recorded problem the second offer solvesStretching delivery before the first service is stableAccount owner with a specialist
New division or region of the same customerA sponsor willing to introduce the firm internallyStarting a new sale without the new buyer's case for changeAccount owner as a new opportunity

The signal column is what a health score should feed. Gainsight's documentation describes scorecards built from weighted measures, such as usage, support and relationship, grouped and combined into one score, with weights that can be redistributed when a measure is missing. A score is only useful for expansion if it has been checked against which past accounts actually grew. Gartner's recommendation for key accounts was similar: monitor relationship health systematically and re-tier accounts on performance, not size.

Expansion into a new division is the motion most often mishandled. It is a new sale to a new buying group, and it needs its own qualification and case for change (Parts 20 and 22). Treating it as an add-on to the existing contract skips both.

Price increases deserve their own decision. A price rise at renewal is a discount decision in reverse, and the same governance applies (Part 21): a reason, an owner, an expected outcome and a review once the renewal closes.

Record every renewal decision

Each renewal is a commercial decision that is frequent, similar to past cases, graded within a contract term and defended by a revenue leader. That makes it a good fit for the decision record described in The commercial decisions worth recording. The record should hold the 90-day decision, its reason, the expected outcome (renewal value, expansion, or loss), the owner and, once known, the result.

Churned and downgraded accounts need the buyer's reason as well as the account owner's. The same mismatch that affects new-business win-loss applies here, so the explainer on win-loss analysis is a useful guide for exit interviews.

After a year of records, the firm can answer questions that most cannot: which risk ratings at 180 days were right, which expansion hypotheses came true, and which health-score measures actually predicted the outcome.

Illustrative example: moving the renewal decision earlier
Decision
Record a renew, change, expand or loss decision for every account 90 days before renewal, with a value review at 120 days.
Reason and owner
Two lost renewals in a quarter had both shown declining usage and an unanswered sponsor change months earlier, but neither had been reviewed until 30 days out. Agreed by the revenue leader; owned by the head of account management.
What changed
Accounts rated at risk at 90 days now get an executive sponsor call and a delivery review. The firm will compare its 90-day ratings with actual outcomes after four quarters and adjust the health score weights accordingly.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B software and services firm with EU customers, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • The base rarely grows by itself. Median net retention near 100% means expansion has to be managed, not waited for.
  • Decide renewals at 90 days. A recorded decision with a reason is what lets the firm learn which accounts it read correctly.
  • Pick the expansion motion by signal. Price, volume, cross-sell and new divisions each need different evidence and owners.
  • Size is not a growth signal. Accounts chosen for their spend alone were less likely to grow in Gartner's research.
Gateway card

Before the next renewal cohort

  • Every renewal in the next two quarters listed with its date and notice period
  • A 180-day review and 120-day value review booked for each
  • A 90-day renewal decision recorded with reason, owner and expected outcome
  • An expansion hypothesis per account, tied to a named signal
  • Notice periods checked against the EU Data Act for any EU cloud or SaaS customer
  • Churn and downgrade reasons collected from the customer, not only the account owner

Common questions

What is a good net revenue retention rate for B2B software?

Benchmarks for private SaaS firms put the median at around 100 to 102%. SaaS Capital found firms at 110% or more grew faster than its sample median, while those below 100% grew more slowly.

When should the renewal process start?

Many firms start around 180 days before the renewal date, with a customer value review at about 120 days and an internal renewal decision at 90 days. Shorter notice periods move the calendar earlier.

What is the difference between upselling and cross-selling at renewal?

Upselling increases what the customer buys of the same product or service, such as seats, usage or tier. Cross-selling adds a different product or service that solves another recorded problem.

How does the EU Data Act affect SaaS renewals?

Since 12 September 2025, customers of data processing services, including SaaS, can switch providers with a maximum notice period of two months, and switching charges must be removed from 12 January 2027, according to legal summaries of the Act.

Sources and notes

  • Sapphire Ventures, KeyBanc Capital Markets and Sapphire Ventures Private SaaS Company Survey, October 2024. Press release on a survey of 100+ private SaaS firms; medians only.
  • SaaS Capital, SaaS Retention Benchmarks for Private B2B Companies, September 2025. Lender's survey; sample size not stated in the article.
  • Growth Unhinged, 2025 SaaS Benchmarks Report, November 2025. Survey of 800+ mostly US SaaS firms with High Alpha; self-reported.
  • Bain & Company, Prescription for cutting costs, Frederick Reichheld, 2001. Consultancy brief; figure is specific to financial services.
  • Gartner, Gartner Survey Shows 95% of Chief Sales Officers Expect Higher Growth From Key Accounts, October 2021. Survey of 69 CSOs; small sample.
  • McKinsey, Five fundamental truths: How B2B winners keep growing, September 2024. Consultancy survey of B2B buyers; switching intent is stated, not observed.
  • Cooley, PaaS, IaaS or SaaS? Be aware: new switching rules will become applicable in EU, September 2025. Law firm summary of the EU Data Act; not legal advice.
  • Gainsight, Measure Weights in Scorecards. Vendor product documentation.

Next move

List every renewal due in the next six months with its notice period. For each one, write down today whether you expect it to renew, change, expand or leave, and why. Check those calls when the renewals close.
